question: In Switzerland, what is the shortest notice period that can validly be agreed for terminating a tenancy?

options.A: One month for residential premises and three months for commercial premises
options.B: Two months for residential premises and four months for commercial premises
options.C: Three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises
options.D: Three months for residential premises only, with no statutory minimum for commercial premises

source_quote: In einem Mietvertrag muss die Kündigungsfrist mindestens drei Monate für Wohnräume und sechs Monate für Geschäftsräume betragen, es können aber auch längere Fristen vereinbart werden.
notes: Source quote is German (official Canton Bern conciliation-authority page); English rendering in the question: in a rental agreement the notice period must be at least three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises, and longer periods may be agreed. Commonly cited German practice of one month's notice plus end-of-month termination is NOT the Swiss rule.

question: A tenant in Switzerland posts their notice of termination on 31 March, and the landlord receives it on 1 April. From when does the notice period run, and when does the termination take effect?

options.A: It runs from 31 March, the date the notice was posted, so the termination takes effect at the end of June
options.B: It runs from 1 April, the date the notice is delivered to the landlord, so the termination takes effect at the end of July
options.C: It runs from 1 April, the date of delivery, so the termination takes effect at the end of June
options.D: It runs from the first day of the calendar month after delivery, so the termination takes effect at the end of August

source_quote: Die Kündigungsfrist läuft erst ab Zustellung der Kündigung an die Vermieterin oder den Vermieter. Wenn Sie also beispielsweise am 31. März die Kündigung verschicken und die Vermieterin oder der Vermieter diese am 1. April erhält, gilt die Kündigung erst auf Ende Juli statt Ende Juni.
notes: German source; English rendering: the notice period only begins on delivery of the notice to the landlord — sent 31 March and received 1 April, it takes effect at the end of July rather than the end of June. Posting date is not decisive.

question: A married couple lives in a Swiss flat, but only one of the spouses is named as the tenant on the rental agreement. Who must sign the letter terminating the tenancy?

options.A: Both spouses must sign the termination, even though only one of them is named as the tenant on the rental agreement
options.B: Only the spouse named as tenant must sign, because only that person is a contracting party
options.C: Only the named tenant signs, but only after obtaining the written consent of the other spouse
options.D: Either spouse may sign alone, and the landlord must accept either signature

source_quote: Wenn Sie als Ehepaar oder eingetragene Partner/innen in der Wohnung wohnen, müssen beide die Kündigung unterschreiben. Dies gilt auch dann, wenn nur eine/r von Ihnen auf dem Mietvertrag als Mieter/in aufgeführt ist.
notes: German source; English rendering: couples who live in the flat as spouses or registered partners must both sign the termination, and this applies even if only one of them is listed as tenant on the rental agreement. Covers registered partners as well as married couples.

question: An EU/EFTA citizen takes a job in Switzerland on an employment contract of unlimited duration. Which Swiss residence permit are they issued, and for how long is it valid?

options.A: An L short-term residence permit, valid for the term of the employment contract
options.B: A C settlement permit, valid for five years
options.C: A G cross-border commuter permit, valid for five years
options.D: A B residence permit, valid for five years

source_quote: The residence permit for EU/EFTA nationals is valid for five years. This permit is issued to EU/EFTA citizens holding a contract of employment of at least twelve months or of unlimited duration.
notes: Switzerland applies its own permit categories to EU/EFTA nationals under the free movement agreement; it is in Schengen but not in the EU, so the EU directive-style permit nomenclature does not apply.

question: For which duration of employment contract is an EU/EFTA national entitled to the Swiss short-term residence permit (category L)?

options.A: A contract of one to three months
options.B: A contract of three to twelve months
options.C: A contract of twelve to twenty-four months
options.D: A contract of twelve months or unlimited duration

source_quote: EU/EFTA nationals are entitled to this permit provided they are in possession of an employment contract valid from three up to twelve months.
notes: The Swiss L permit is defined by the employment-contract term, not by a 90-day short-stay rule as in EU free-movement law. Contracts of under three months within a calendar year need no permit at all, only the online notification procedure (separate fact, not tested here).

question: After five years of regular and uninterrupted residence in Switzerland, which nationals are granted settlement permits pursuant to settlement treaties or reciprocal agreements?

options.A: All nationals of all EU and EFTA member states, once they have completed five years' residence
options.B: Only EFTA nationals — Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway
options.C: Nationals of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, as well as EFTA nationals (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway)
options.D: Only nationals of the EU member states that acceded to the EU most recently

source_quote: If they meet the required conditions, nationals of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden as well as EFTA nationals (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway) are granted settlement permits pursuant to settlement treaties or reciprocal agreements after five years' regular and uninterrupted residence in Switzerland.
notes: Switzerland holds bilateral settlement agreements with 15 EU states plus the three EFTA states; the source states expressly that no such treaties exist for the nationals of the other EU member states. SEM sets the earliest date from which settlement permits may be granted.

question: A holder of a Swiss EU/EFTA cross-border commuter permit (category G) lives in a neighbouring EU state and works in Switzerland. How often must they return to their main place of residence abroad?

options.A: As a rule every day, or at least once a week
options.B: At least once a month
options.C: At least once every six months
options.D: Only when the permit is renewed or its validity is extended

source_quote: Cross-border commuters must return to their main place of residence abroad as a rule every day, or at least once a week.
notes: Category G has no direct EU equivalent; it is the Swiss instrument for EU/EFTA nationals who live abroad and work in Switzerland, whether employed or self-employed.

question: Under Swiss federal law, what residence requirement must be met before applying for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: At least five years of residence, including one of the two years preceding the application
options.B: At least ten years of residence, all of it within the five years preceding the application
options.C: At least fifteen years of residence, including five of the ten years preceding the application
options.D: At least ten years of residence, including three of the five years prior to the application being made

source_quote: Federal law requires you to have lived in Switzerland for at least ten years, including three of the five years prior to the application being made.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: on top of the federal ten-year rule, each canton sets an additional requirement of between two and five years' residence in the particular commune or canton, and each commune makes its own rules within cantonal and federal law. Those extra conditions are deliberately not tested here.

question: For ordinary naturalisation in Switzerland, how is time spent in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 treated, and when can the applicant first apply?

options.A: It counts once, and no application is possible until at least ten years of total residence
options.B: It counts double, but no application is possible until at least six years of total residence in the country
options.C: It counts double, but no application is possible until at least twelve years of total residence
options.D: It counts double, but no application is possible before the applicant reaches the age of 18

source_quote: The time spent in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 counts double, but you cannot apply for naturalisation until you have lived in the country for at least six years.
notes: The six-year floor is the earliest any application may be made and is a separate condition from the ten-year federal requirement tested in K028.

question: Which Swiss residence permit must a foreign citizen already hold before being able to apply for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: A short-term residence permit (L)
options.B: A residence permit (B)
options.C: A settlement permit (C)
options.D: A cross-border commuter permit (G)

source_quote: Holders of a settlement permit (C permit)
notes: Ordinary naturalisation is restricted to holders of a C permit; the residency periods themselves are tested separately. Simplified naturalisation is open to other categories (spouse or child of a Swiss citizen, stateless minor, third-generation residents under 25).

question: How long is a Swiss provisional (learner) driving licence valid for category B (cars), compared with category A (motorcycles)?

options.A: 12 months for cars and 6 months for motorcycles
options.B: 24 months for cars and for motorcycles alike
options.C: 36 months for cars and 12 months for motorcycles
options.D: 24 months for cars and 4 months for motorcycles

source_quote: The provisional licence is valid for 24 months for cars (category B) and for 4 months for motorcycles (category A).
notes: The motorcycle figure is strikingly short compared with the car figure; the provisional licence is also valid only in Switzerland.

question: In Switzerland, what conditions must a person meet in order to accompany a learner driver on a drive?

options.A: They must be at least 23 years old, have passed their driving test at least three years previously, and no longer hold a probationary driving licence
options.B: They must be at least 21 years old and have held a full driving licence for at least one year
options.C: They must be at least 25 years old and have held a full category B licence for at least five years
options.D: They must be at least 18 years old, provided they have not been disqualified from driving in the previous two years

source_quote: The accompanying person must be at least 23 years old, have passed their driving test at least three years previously and must no longer have a probationary driving licence.
notes: Three cumulative conditions: age, three years since passing the driving test, and no longer being on a probationary licence. Learner drivers may not have drunk alcohol before driving; the legal limit is a blood alcohol level of over 0.01%.

question: A learner obtains a Swiss provisional driving licence on their 19th birthday. How long must they wait before they may take the practical driving test?

options.A: Six months
options.B: At least twelve months
options.C: At least twenty-four months
options.D: No fixed waiting period, once the compulsory traffic skills course has been attended

source_quote: If you get your provisional licence before your 20th birthday, you will need to wait at least 12 months before you can take the practical driving test.
notes: The 12-month wait is conditional on the provisional licence having been issued before the 20th birthday; the compulsory eight-hour traffic skills course is a separate precondition for registering for the test.

question: In Switzerland, on which tax bases do the three taxing levels — the Confederation, the cantons and the communes — levy taxes on private individuals?

options.A: All three levels levy taxes on both income and assets
options.B: The Confederation taxes income only, the cantons tax assets only, and the communes tax both income and assets
options.C: The Confederation taxes assets only, while the cantons and communes tax income only
options.D: The Confederation levies direct federal tax on income, while the cantons and communes levy taxes on both income and assets

source_quote: The cantons and the communes levy their taxes on both the income and the assets of private individuals.
notes: The page deliberately carries no CHF figures, rates or brackets; the Confederation taxes income only, whereas the two sub-national levels tax income and wealth. No rate may be presented as a nationwide figure.

question: Two neighbouring communes in the same Swiss canton can levy different tax rates on an identical household income. What accounts for the difference?

options.A: Each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these co-efficients can vary considerably
options.B: Each canton sets a separate statutory tax rate for each individual commune within it
options.C: The Confederation adds a municipal surtax that differs from commune to commune
options.D: The statutory tax rate is fixed by federal law but is waived by individual communes

source_quote: Because each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these can vary considerably, there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within the same canton.
notes: COMMUNAL-VARIABLE: the co-efficient is changed from time to time, so no specific value is permanent. This is why there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within a single canton — a distinctly Swiss feature of communal tax autonomy.

question: What is the minimum annual holiday entitlement for a worker in Switzerland who is under 20 years old?

options.A: Four weeks
options.B: Three weeks
options.C: Five weeks
options.D: Six weeks

source_quote: Up to the age of 20, you are entitled to at least five weeks' vacation.
notes: The general statutory minimum for all workers is four weeks regardless of full- or part-time; the entitlement rises to at least five weeks up to the age of 20, and more may be agreed. Distinct from the public-holiday facts carried by S031.

question: In Switzerland, may an employee decide unilaterally when to take their statutory annual leave?

options.A: Yes — the statutory entitlement is unconditional, so the employee alone fixes the dates
options.B: No — the employer must approve the time off, and may require the employee to change dates that are not compatible with the needs or interests of the company
options.C: No — leave may only be taken in the calendar year in which it was earned
options.D: Yes, provided one month's notice is given to the employer in advance

source_quote: You need your employer's approval to take time off. If your holidays are not compatible with the needs or interests of the company, your boss can ask you to change them.
notes: This is the fact that appears on S013 but not on the shared S031 page; keeping it here avoids duplicating the public-holiday facts.

question: For a residential rental in Switzerland, what is the maximum rental deposit (security deposit) a landlord may require?

options.A: One month's rent
options.B: Two months' rent
options.C: Three months' rent
options.D: There is no statutory maximum

source_quote: Rental deposit, also known as a security deposit: This must only be paid when required in the agreement. For residential rentals, this is a maximum of three months' rent.
notes: The deposit may be demanded only if the agreement provides for it; three months' rent is a ceiling, not an entitlement.

question: What biometric data does the microchip in a Swiss biometric residence permit for foreign nationals store, and for how long?

options.A: One digital fingerprint and a facial image, stored for five years
options.B: Two digital fingerprints and a facial image, stored for ten years
options.C: A facial image and the holder's passport number, stored for three years
options.D: Two digital fingerprints and a facial image, stored for five years

source_quote: an embedded microchip with biometric data: two digital fingerprints and a facial image. The data are stored for five years and may only be used for the purpose of issuing a new biometric residence permit without the need for additional data processing.
notes: The stored data may be used only to issue a new biometric residence permit. The chip does not allow a person to be located or monitored. CANTONAL-VARIABLE: application and issuance are decided by the canton of residence.

question: When did Switzerland sign the Schengen Agreement, and when was a microchip for storing biometric data added to the new credit-card-format residence permit?

options.A: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, and the microchip was added in early 2011
options.B: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, and the microchip was added in 2009
options.C: Switzerland acceded to the Schengen acquis in 2004, and the microchip was added in early 2011
options.D: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 15 March 2008, and the microchip was added in early 2013

source_quote: When it signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, Switzerland began issuing a new residence permit in credit-card format to foreign nationals. In a subsequent development in early 2011, a microchip was added to these residence permits for the purpose of storing biometric data.
notes: Switzerland joined Schengen in 2008 while remaining outside the EU and the EEA. Presented with a valid national passport, the biometric residence permit entitles the holder to travel throughout the Schengen area without a visa.

question: Under Swiss data protection law, what is actually protected?

options.A: The data themselves, as an asset of whoever holds them
options.B: The persons about whom data are processed
options.C: The commercial value of the collected information
options.D: Only special categories of personal data, such as health and criminal records

source_quote: Data protection law does not protect data as such, but rather the persons about whom data is processed.
notes: Traps the property-framing imported from data-protection-as-asset models; the FDPIC states the protection attaches to persons, not to the data as a commodity.

question: Under the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP), whose processing of personal data is regulated?

options.A: Federal authorities only, with private companies left entirely to cantonal law
options.B: Private companies only, since the Confederation has no supervisory role
options.C: Both federal authorities and private individuals or legal entities, including associations and commercial enterprises
options.D: Only cantonal and communal authorities, since data protection is a cantonal matter

source_quote: It contains legal norms that serve the protection of personality and informational self-determination and regulate the processing of personal data carried out by federal authorities or private individuals or legal entities (e.g. associations or commercial enterprises).
notes: The FADP reaches private companies as well as federal bodies. The distractor A imports the idea that data protection is a purely public-sector or cantonal matter.

question: Under Swiss law, how does the processing of personal data by private entities generally stand?

options.A: It is prohibited unless the data subject has given prior written consent
options.B: It is permitted only where the data have been fully anonymised
options.C: It requires prior authorisation from the FDPIC for each processing purpose
options.D: It is permitted in principle, with the test being whether the invasion of privacy can be justified by consent or by overriding interests

source_quote: The situation is different for the processing of personal data by private entities. In principle, this is permitted in Switzerland.
notes: Distractor A is the GDPR prior-consent default, which does not carry over to Swiss private-sector processing; the source deliberately does not use the words opt-in or opt-out.

question: Where the Swiss State processes personal data, how do the citizen's data protection rights stand?

options.A: The citizen may waive them in an individual case once the authority holds their written consent
options.B: They apply only to data processed by private companies, not to federal bodies
options.C: There is in principle no voluntary waiver, and the purpose, scope and extent of state processing are fixed by statute
options.D: They may be waived by a cantonal court at the authority's request

source_quote: The protection of privacy is a constitutionally guaranteed fundamental right (Art. 13 of the Federal Constitution). In principle, there is no voluntary waiver of data protection rights with regard to the processing of personal data by the State.
notes: Distractor A transplants the private-sector consent logic into the public-law sphere, where the FDPIC says no waiver is possible.

question: A Swiss company gathers personal data about an employee from a third party rather than from the employee. What does the FADP require of the company?

options.A: To inform the data subject in advance and in an adequate manner that their data are to be gathered
options.B: Nothing, because the data were not obtained from the data subject
options.C: Prior notification to the cantonal data protection authority
options.D: Notice within one month of the processing, at the latest

source_quote: Whenever personal data is gathered, the data controller must inform the data subject in advance and in an adequate manner that their data is to be gathered, even if the data are not gathered directly from the data subject concerned.
notes: The duty to inform bites on indirect collection too, and it bites in advance rather than after processing. Distractor D weakens advance notice to a post-hoc deadline.

question: The duty to inform under Swiss data protection law is not absolute. How are its exceptions treated?

options.A: They are drawn broadly by the FDPIC and may be relied on at the controller's discretion
options.B: They cover, for example, a data subject who already has the information or processing required by law, and they must be narrowly interpreted
options.C: They apply only where a federal authority processes the data
options.D: They apply only to special categories of data such as health data

source_quote: Moreover, the exceptions mentioned in Article 20 FADP limit or remove the duty to provide information, for example if a data subject already has the information (because they previously consented to their data being processed) or if the processing of personal data is required by law. These exceptions must be narrowly interpreted: the data controller should not assume that they will apply.
notes: Names the Article 20 FADP exceptions and the narrow-interpretation rule; distractor A is the opposite of the FDPIC's express warning against assuming they apply.

question: How does the Swiss Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) differ from its EU counterparts?

options.A: It can impose administrative fines of up to 5 per cent of annual turnover
options.B: It can suspend a company's data processing for up to twelve months
options.C: It may order the deletion of any unlawfully processed data without any court involvement
options.D: It has no power to impose sanctions under the FADP, so fines of up to CHF 250,000 fall on the natural person responsible for the offence

source_quote: Fines of up to CHF250,000 may be imposed on the natural person responsible for the offence. Legal persons can be fined up to CHF50,000, only as a subsidiary measure.
notes: Distractors A and C are GDPR-style supervisory powers the FDPIC does not have under the FADP; enforcement runs through binding orders and the FADP's criminal provisions.

question: May a private individual in Switzerland operate CCTV systems covering public property?

options.A: No, such systems are normally regarded as an excessive and unlawful measure and their installation is prohibited
options.B: Yes, provided the monitored area is clearly signposted
options.C: Yes, if the cameras operate only at night
options.D: Only with a cantonal permit, which is routinely granted for crime prevention

source_quote: As a result, private CCTV systems in public areas are normally regarded as an excessive and unlawful measure and their installation is prohibited.
notes: Public-space video surveillance is handled under cantonal and communal law with private systems generally barred; signage alone does not make a private public-space camera lawful.

question: A shopkeeper installs cameras covering the pavement outside the shop to deter burglars. Why does this fail under Swiss data protection guidance?

options.A: Because a private camera may never record any area beyond the owner's own property
options.B: Because preserving security and order in public areas is a task for the police, not for private individuals
options.C: Because only a cantonal authority may install cameras under a communal ordinance
options.D: Because shopkeepers must first exhaust every less intrusive security measure

source_quote: Interest in crime prevention: the preservation of security and order in public areas is not the responsibility of private individuals, but a task for the police. For this reason, protecting his or her own security is not a legitimate reason for a private individual to monitor a public area.
notes: Self-protection is expressly not a legitimate reason for a private person to monitor a public area, because that task belongs to the police.

question: When is private surveillance that incidentally records a public area normally tolerated in Switzerland?

options.A: Whenever it protects the person's own property, however much of the public area is captured
options.B: Whenever the footage is deleted within 24 hours
options.C: Whenever a neighbouring resident gives written consent
options.D: When the intrusion on the public area is negligible and surveillance of the private property would otherwise be impossible

source_quote: There are possible exceptions to this rule: When legitimate video surveillance of private property is conducted, images of public areas are also recorded. If the extent of this intrusion is negligible and the surveillance of the private property would otherwise be impossible, common sense dictates that surveillance will normally be allowed.
notes: Two cumulative conditions: negligible intrusion plus impossibility of surveillance otherwise. Distractor B lifts the retention figure and mistakes a storage rule for a permission rule.

question: A private individual wants to install a camera that would also cover a public area. With whose authority must the question of permission be settled in advance?

options.A: The commune, with which it must be clarified in advance whether permission is required
options.B: The FDPIC, which grants or refuses the permit
options.C: The cantonal police, which approve the installation as a crime-prevention measure
options.D: The cantonal building authority, under cantonal building law

source_quote: If public places are involved, it must be clarified in advance with the commune whether permission is required. Monitored areas must be clearly signposted.
notes: This is the cantonally anchored level: the commune decides, not a federal permit office. Distractors B and D transplant federal or building-law approval routes.

question: For how long should footage from video surveillance be retained in Switzerland?

options.A: Indefinitely, provided the footage is stored on an access-protected drive
options.B: For up to six months, so that incidents can still be traced
options.C: As a general rule it should be deleted within 24 to 72 hours, the period depending on the purpose of the monitoring
options.D: For exactly 24 hours in every case, with no variation permitted

source_quote: Recordings should only be retained for a limited period. The length of time the data is kept depends on the purpose of the monitoring. As a general rule, recordings should be deleted within 24 to 72 hours.
notes: The window is a 24-72 hour range, not a fixed deadline; distractor D hard-codes the lower bound and distractor B imports a German-style retention period.

question: Which residence permit categories are issued as biometric residence permits for foreign nationals in Switzerland?

options.A: Short-term residence permits (L), residence permits (B) and settlement permits (C)
options.B: All residence permits without exception, including the N permit for asylum seekers and the F permit for provisionally admitted foreigners
options.C: Only residence permits (B), because short stays are covered by a passport stamp
options.D: Only settlement permits (C), since biometric data are required for a permanent status

source_quote: Biometric residence permits shall be issued to holders of the following categories of residence permit: - Short-term residence permits (L) - Residence permits (B) - Settlement permits (C)
notes: Exactly the three categories L, B and C; the N and F permits are deliberately not in the biometric programme.

question: Who decides the application procedure for a biometric residence permit in Switzerland, and who captures the biometric data?

options.A: The SEM decides nationally, and the fingerprints are taken at the Swiss embassy
options.B: The municipality of residence decides, and the data are captured by the cantonal police
options.C: The FDPIC decides, and the data are captured by an accredited private provider
options.D: The canton of residence decides, and the biometric data are captured by that canton's authority

source_quote: The application procedure and issuance of a biometric residence permit are decided by the Canton of residence. Biometric data are obtained from the person by the corresponding authority in the Canton of residence.
notes: Cantonal variable: no single national procedure or fee. Distractor A overstates the SEM's role, which is limited to centrally producing the cards.

question: What happens to a first-generation Swiss residence permit for foreign nationals that carries no biometric data?

options.A: It becomes invalid as soon as the holder applies for a biometric permit
options.B: It is automatically upgraded to a settlement permit after five years
options.C: It remains valid until its expiry date, a biometric permit being issued only once it has expired or if personal data change
options.D: It must be surrendered within six months of the holder's first entry into Switzerland

source_quote: First-generation residence permits for foreign nationals (i.e. no biometric data stored) shall remain valid until the expiry date. The new biometric residence permit shall only be issued after the previous residence permit has expired or if changes in personal data require issuance of a new residence permit.
notes: Transition rule, not a revocation rule; distractor B invents an automatic five-year upgrade that the page does not support.

question: Who must sign the letter terminating a Swiss rental agreement, and how should it be sent to the landlord?

options.A: Only the first-named tenant, sent by ordinary post
options.B: All parties who signed the rental agreement, with the letter sent to the landlord by registered mail
options.C: Every adult occupant of the flat, sent by registered mail, whether or not they signed the agreement
options.D: Any one of the tenants, since one signature binds all signatories

source_quote: All parties who signed the rental agreement must sign the letter of termination. Tenants who are renting with a spouse or registered partner must have the approval of the other person to terminate the agreement, even if only one party has signed the agreement as the tenant. Tenants are not required to provide a reason for terminating the agreement. The letter of termination should be sent to the landlord by registered mail.
notes: Two traps: signature is required from all signatories (not all occupants), and proof of dispatch matters, so registered mail is the safe route. The tenant need give no reason.

question: How long does a tenant in Switzerland have to contact the commune's conciliation authority in order to contest a termination?

options.A: 14 days, running from the date the letter of termination is posted
options.B: 3 months, matching the statutory notice period for residential premises
options.C: There is no fixed deadline, because each cantonal conciliation authority sets its own
options.D: 30 days

source_quote: Tenants have 30 days to contact their commune's conciliation authority to contest the termination.
notes: The 30-day contestation window is distinct from the notice period itself, which distractor B conflates with it.

question: Under Swiss tenancy rules, when may a tenant sublet a furnished apartment and add a surcharge to the monthly rent?

options.A: A surcharge of up to 20% of the monthly rent may be added, to compensate for wear and tear on furnishings
options.B: A surcharge of up to 50% of the monthly rent may be added, once the landlord has been informed
options.C: No surcharge at all may be added; the subletting tenant may charge only what they themselves pay
options.D: A surcharge of up to 10% of the monthly rent may be added, but only for a fixed-term lease

source_quote: A maximum surcharge of 20% may be added to the monthly rent on a furnished apartment, to compensate for wear and tear on furnishings. In all other cases, tenants may only charge what they themselves pay for the apartment (incl. additional charges).
notes: The 20% allowance is confined to furnished apartments; distractor C states the rule for all other cases and drops the furnished exception.

question: In Switzerland, on what grounds is a landlord generally permitted to terminate a rental agreement?

options.A: Only for reasons listed in the tenancy act, such as non-payment of rent
options.B: For any reason in principle, with no requirement to observe any notice period
options.C: For any reason in principle, but the statutory or contractual notice period must be observed and an official form must be used
options.D: Only with the prior authorisation of the cantonal conciliation authority

source_quote: In Switzerland, landlords are generally allowed to terminate a rental agreement for any reason. They are nevertheless required to observe the notice periods stated in law or in the agreement, and to use an official form to terminate the agreement.
notes: Swiss law is cause-free for landlords but procedural: notice period plus official form. Distractor A imports the German cause requirement, distractor B drops the formalities.

question: An EU/EFTA national who is not in gainful employment wishes to obtain a Swiss B residence permit. What must such a person show?

options.A: That they have been resident in Switzerland for at least five years
options.B: That they have sufficient financial means and adequate health and accident insurance
options.C: That they hold a job offer of at least twelve months' duration
options.D: That a Swiss employer guarantees their residence for the full five-year period

source_quote: Nationals from all EU/EFTA member states without gainful employment are entitled to a B permit if they can prove they have sufficient financial means and adequate health and accident insurance.
notes: Distractors A and C apply residence-duration or employment-contract thresholds that belong to other permit categories; the non-employed B route is insurance and means, not job history.

question: An EU/EFTA national's B residence permit comes up for renewal after more than twelve consecutive months of involuntary unemployment. How may that first renewal be dealt with?

options.A: It may be limited to one year
options.B: It cannot be granted at all, because the holder no longer has gainful employment
options.C: It must be reduced to the three-month minimum used for short-stay permits
options.D: It is automatically replaced by an L permit issued to job seekers

source_quote: First-time renewal of the permit can be limited to one year, however, if the holder has been involuntarily unemployed for more than twelve consecutive months.
notes: A shortening mechanism, not a withdrawal rule. Distractors B and D over-read the unemployment fact into loss of status or an automatic category change.

question: An EU/EFTA national takes up a series of engagements in Switzerland, none lasting longer than three months. How are these handled?

options.A: Each engagement requires its own work permit of up to three months
options.B: A G cross-border commuter permit is required throughout
options.C: A B residence permit valid for twelve months is required
options.D: Contracts of less than three months' duration within a calendar year are not subject to a permit but are regulated via the online notification procedure

source_quote: Employment contracts of less than three months' duration within a calendar year are not subject to a permit but are regulated via the online notification procedure.
notes: The Swiss online notification procedure replaces a permit for short engagements below three months within a calendar year; the boundary is three months, not one year.

question: In Switzerland, which authority assesses the taxes and collects the direct federal tax as well as cantonal and communal taxes?

options.A: The Federal Tax Administration, for all three taxing levels
options.B: Each commune, which collects the federal share and passes it on to the canton
options.C: The cantons, which calculate the taxes and collect the federal taxes as well as cantonal and communal taxes
options.D: The FDPIC, which supervises the assessment of tax

source_quote: The cantonal tax authorities calculate your taxes on the basis of the figures you provide in your tax return. The cantons collect both the federal taxes and the cantonal and communal taxes.
notes: Counterintuitive: the cantons are the collecting and assessing authority for the federal tax as well, which distractor A assigns to the Federal Tax Administration.

question: On what basis are Swiss taxes calculated?

options.A: On total gross income, with no deductions permitted before assessment
options.B: On 'taxable income', a lower amount from which social insurance contributions and other permissible deductions have been subtracted
options.C: On gross income less social insurance contributions only, with no other deductions allowed
options.D: On taxable wealth, with income taxed only by the Confederation

source_quote: Taxes are not calculated on the basis of your total income, but on the basis of what is known as your 'taxable income'. This is a lower amount. You can deduct social insurance contributions from your income and make various other deductions in your tax return.
notes: Distractor D reverts to the federal/communal split of tax bases (income for the Confederation, income and wealth for cantons and communes), which is not the rule for computing the bill.

question: Which single day is Switzerland's only national public holiday?

options.A: 1 August
options.B: 1 January
options.C: 1 August and 25 December
options.D: Ascension Day

source_quote: The first of August - Swiss national day - is Switzerland's only national public holiday.
notes: Everything else is cantonal; 25 December and 1 January are cantonal holidays, not national ones.

question: Beyond Switzerland's single national public holiday, who determines the other public holidays observed in a canton?

options.A: The federal government, which publishes a national list each year
options.B: Each canton, which can have up to eight additional public holidays on its territory
options.C: Each commune alone, with no upper limit and no cantonal role
options.D: The cantons and communes jointly, up to a federal ceiling of eight

source_quote: The cantons can each have up to eight additional public holidays on their territory. Public holidays can thus vary from canton to canton.
notes: Eight is a ceiling on the cantonal additions, not a nationwide total of public holidays; distractor D misreads it as a federal maximum.

question: Under Swiss tenancy law, how may a tenant end the tenancy before the notice period or the contractual termination date has expired?

options.A: By paying a penalty equal to three months' rent
options.B: By giving three months' notice and paying the rent until the next customary termination date
options.C: By cumulatively proposing a suitable replacement tenant who will take over on the same conditions and returning the rented property
options.D: By obtaining a release from the cantonal conciliation authority

source_quote: Sie können das Mietverhältnis vor Ablauf einer festen Vertragsdauer, der Kündigungsfrist oder einem Kündigungstermin beenden, wenn Sie der Vermieterin oder dem Vermieter kumulativ - eine Nachmieterin oder einen Nachmieter vorschlagen, der/die den Mietvertrag zu den gleichen Bedingungen übernehmen will und zumutbar ist, und - das Mietobjekt zurückgeben.
notes: Source quote is German (Canton Bern conciliation authority). English: the tenancy may be ended early only if the tenant cumulatively proposes a suitable replacement tenant taking over on the same conditions and returns the rented property. Both limbs are required.

question: According to the Canton Bern conciliation authority, when is an ordinary termination of a tenancy possible?

options.A: Only if the notice period and the locally customary termination dates are observed
options.B: On one month's notice, aligned to the end of a calendar month
options.C: Only with the prior consent of the conciliation authority
options.D: Only for a fixed-term contract, never for an open-ended one

source_quote: Die ordentliche Kündigung ist nur unter Einhaltung der Kündigungsfrist und der Kündigungstermine möglich.
notes: Source quote is German. The source states the locally customary termination dates, not a universal end-of-month rule, so distractor B is the widely repeated but unverified one-month claim.

question: How long is the probationary period on a newly acquired Swiss category B driving licence, and what follows a serious traffic violation?

options.A: Two years, extended by six months after a serious violation
options.B: Three years, extended by one year where a serious traffic violation leads to disqualification from driving
options.C: Three years, during which any serious violation ends the licence permanently
options.D: Five years, extended by one year for each serious traffic violation

source_quote: The probationary period lasts three years. If you commit a serious traffic violation during this period and are disqualified from driving, the probationary period will be extended by one year.
notes: Extension by one year, and only where disqualification from driving follows; distractor C confuses extension with revocation.

question: In Switzerland, what is the fee for simplified naturalisation of an adult, and what happens to it if the application is refused?

options.A: CHF 900, and the full amount must be paid in advance and is not refunded if the application is refused
options.B: CHF 650, refundable if the application is refused
options.C: CHF 250, the same rate as for minors under the age of 12
options.D: Up to CHF 2,000, set by the canton and refunded on refusal

source_quote:
The cost of simplified naturalisation in Switzerland varies according to age:
- 250 francs for minors under the age of 12
- 650 francs for minors aged 12 and over
- 900 francs for adults.
For spouses of Swiss citizens residing abroad, simplified naturalisation costs 600 francs.
The full amount must be paid in advance and is not refunded if the application is refused.
notes: CHF 900 is the adult rate, distinct from the 12-and-over minor rate of 650 and the under-12 rate of 250; CHF 2,000 is the cantonal fee for ordinary naturalisation, not this one.
